Revert "Cache user profile lookups in Redis"

This reverts commit 4f2c9ab.

The cache had no invalidation on write, so profile updates landed in Postgres
while reads kept serving the old row for the full 15m TTL. Users saw their old
name and avatar after saving, and support picked up the reports.

Reverting to restore correctness. Re-land once we invalidate on write instead
of waiting for TTL expiry.

## Summary

Checkout was unavailable for 40 minutes on 12 August, from 14:12 to 14:52 UTC. The TLS certificate on our payment gateway expired at 14:12, and every checkout request failed the handshake at the edge from that second onward. Customers could still browse and add to cart, but no order could be completed.

Roughly 1,840 checkout attempts failed, representing about $62,000 in blocked orders. No data was lost or corrupted, and no card data was exposed at any point.

The certificate had a 90-day lifetime and automatic renewal. Renewal had been silently failing since 14 June, when the ACME account credentials were rotated as part of an unrelated cleanup and the renewal job was never updated. Our expiry monitoring covered public web domains but not the internal gateway hostname, so nothing alerted before customers did.

Recovery took 40 minutes: 22 minutes to identify the expired certificate as the cause, and 18 to issue and deploy a replacement. The first 22 minutes were spent on the payment provider, because the error surfaced as a generic gateway failure with no mention of TLS.

We're hiring our first design engineer.

What that means: you own how the product feels, end to end. Design the interaction, then build it in React. No handoff doc, no ticket ping-pong, no waiting for someone else to get the animation almost right.

Small team, real users, and a product currently held together with good intentions and some mediocre CSS. If you've wanted the whole loop in your own hands, this is that job.

Remote-friendly, details in the comments. Tag someone who should see it.

Hey Sam, nudging you on this one, it's been sitting three days and the billing work behind it is blocked: [link]

It's about 200 lines and the only tricky part is the retry logic in the middle, the rest is plumbing. If this week is packed just tell me and I'll find another reviewer, genuinely no hard feelings.

**Timestamp every step of one deploy before you change anything**, a single run with per-step timing tells you more than a week of theories.

**1 → Get the breakdown first.** Most CI systems already report duration per step. If yours doesn't, wrap each stage in a timestamp echo. You want one table: checkout, dependency install, build, tests, image push, rollout, health check. That table is the whole investigation.

**2 → Expect the time to sit in one of three places.** Dependency install on a cold cache, the test suite, or the rollout wait (health checks, connection draining, batch size). In a 25 minute deploy, one of these is usually 10 minutes or more on its own.

**3 → Separate "slow" from "waiting on purpose".** Rollout soak periods and health check windows are configured delays, not slowness. Cutting a 5 minute health check to 90 seconds is a config change you can do this afternoon. Cutting a 9 minute test suite is a quarter of work. Know which one you're buying before you commit.

**4 → Measure across 5 to 10 deploys, not one.** Cache hit versus miss swings install time by minutes, so a single run will point you at the wrong bottleneck.

**Warning: the dread usually isn't the 25 minutes.** It's not knowing whether it will work and not being able to undo it quickly. Time your rollback too. If rollback is itself a 25 minute redeploy, fix that first, it buys more calm than shaving the build ever will.

**Turn it on, but per-file, never repo-wide in one PR.** Strict mode in a large codebase is only a trap if you try to fix everything at once.

**1 → Set `strict: true` globally, then exempt the existing mess.** New and touched files are strict from day one, legacy files opt out with `// @ts-nocheck` or a scoped `include`. Old code keeps compiling, and the pile stops growing today.

**2 → If the error count is frightening, enable the sub-flags one at a time.** `strict` is 8 flags in a trenchcoat. `noImplicitAny` is usually the cheapest first win. `strictNullChecks` finds the most real bugs and also produces most of the errors, so give it its own PR.

**3 → Ratchet instead of sprinting.** Record the current error count in a file and fail CI if it increases. The backlog drains during normal feature work, and you never have to ask for a three-week freeze that nobody will fund.

**Warning: don't silence `strictNullChecks` with `!`.** The non-null assertion satisfies the compiler and keeps the bug, and it's the default reflex when someone is 400 errors deep. Adding a real guard where code used to throw is a behavior change, so review those diffs rather than autopiloting them.

**The actual trap is the big-bang branch.** A months-long "strict migration" branch conflicts with everything and dies unmerged. If someone proposes that, say no to the branch, not to strict mode.

**A cache is a second copy of your data, and every invalidation strategy is just a different answer to "when does the copy become a lie?"** With a database alone there's one truth. The moment you cache, there are two, and they drift.

**1 → TTL: the copy expires on a timer.** You say "keep this for 60 seconds" and after that the next read goes back to the database. Dead simple, and it's where most people should start. The price is explicit: for up to 60 seconds you knowingly serve data that may be wrong.

**2 → Delete-on-write: you remove the cached copy whenever you write.** The next read refills it from the database. Deleting beats updating the cached copy in place, because keeping two copies correct in two code paths is exactly where the bugs live. This gets you near-instant correctness, and it only works if every write path routes through that code, including migrations, admin tools, and scripts.

**3 → Tag-based: throw away a group at once.** You tag entries ("everything about user 42") and drop the whole tag when anything about user 42 changes. Worth it when one write invalidates fifty cached views. More machinery, fewer missed spots.

**4 → Versioned keys: never invalidate, just stop asking.** Put a version in the key (`user:42:v7`). A write bumps it to v8, and the v7 entry is orphaned and expires on its own. No delete to race against, at the cost of holding garbage until it ages out.

**The gotcha that catches everyone: the read and the write interleave.** A reader misses the cache and fetches the old row. The writer updates the row and deletes the cache. Then the slow reader writes its already-stale value in. The cache is now wrong with no event coming to fix it. This is why almost every cache keeps a TTL even with perfect invalidation. The TTL is the floor under your mistakes, keep it.

**Practical starting point:** short TTL plus delete-on-write. Add tags or versions only after you can point at a specific stale-read incident that they would have prevented.

**Fix the pages before you touch the rota**, six people cannot rotate their way out of noisy alerting.

**1 → Count what actually woke people up last month.** Export every page, group by alert name. In most burning-out teams, 3 to 5 alerts produce more than half the pages, and a large share needed no action at all. That list is your plan, and it takes an hour to make.

**2 → Delete or de-page every alert that didn't need a human at 3am.** If the response was "acknowledged, went back to sleep", it becomes a ticket or a dashboard. This is the highest-leverage change available to you and it costs nothing.

**3 → With six people, one week in six is the ceiling of sustainable, and only if nights are quiet.** If people are being woken on multiple nights per rotation, lengthening the cycle won't help, the noise is the problem. Check that math before you promise anyone relief.

**4 → Take the on-call person off sprint commitments for their week.** Carrying feature deadlines while on-call is the specific thing that breaks people. Their official job that week is interrupts, toil reduction, and killing the top alert from step 1.

**5 → Pay back lost sleep the same week, automatically.** Woken after midnight means start late or take the day, written down, no asking required. If it needs permission, nobody will take it.

**Warning: don't let a hero absorb extra shifts.** It works for a quarter, then you lose them, and their pages land on five people who are already tired.

**Also found:** if some of the six can't resolve incidents alone, your real rotation is smaller than six. Fix runbooks and access gaps first, or widening the rota just funnels the wake-ups back to the same two people.

**1% is roughly normal for a free tier, so the useful question isn't whether it's good, it's where people stop.** Pricing problems and product problems look identical in that number and completely different in the funnel.

**1 → Split by activation before anything else.** Take only users who reached your core action, the thing the product exists to do, and compute their conversion separately. Activated users at 15% and everyone else at 0.2% means onboarding, not price. Activated users at 2% means pricing or packaging.

**2 → Check whether anyone ever hits the wall.** Measure what share of active free users reach a free tier limit. If almost nobody does, your free tier is too generous and there's no reason to pay, which is a packaging fix, not a price cut. If many hit it and still don't pay, the value at that wall isn't worth what you're asking.

**3 → Look at pricing page traffic and drop-off.** Lots of people viewing pricing and not buying points at price or plan confusion. Almost nobody reaching the pricing page at all points at the product never getting good enough to consider.

**4 → Talk to 10 people who hit the limit and didn't upgrade.** Fastest signal in the whole exercise. It's also the only way to hear "I couldn't tell which plan I needed", which reads as a pricing problem in the data and is actually a page problem.

**Warning: don't cut the price to test this.** It moves the number slightly, tells you nothing about which cause you had, and is very hard to walk back. Test packaging, meaning what's free and what's behind the wall, before you touch the number.

**Also found:** check conversion by acquisition source. One cheap channel sending unqualified signups can drag a healthy 4% down to 1% with nothing wrong with either your product or your price.

**Tell the team yourself before the rumor does, this week is about the people staying, not the one leaving.**

**1 → Today: say it plainly.** What happened, when they finish, and that you are not backfilling in a panic. Two days of silence gets filled with "who's next", and that's much harder to walk back than the news itself.

**2 → This week: one-on-one with every person, and ask directly.** "How are you feeling about this?" and then be quiet. You're listening for whether this is one person leaving or the first of three. If two people echo the same complaint, that's your real problem and it just became urgent.

**3 → Don't counter-offer.** People who accept one usually leave within a year anyway, and the team learns that resigning is how you get a raise. If their reasons surface something fixable, fix it for the people still here instead.

**4 → Start knowledge transfer now, targeted.** Ask them for the list of things only they know, then pair them with a named person on the top three. A general "please document everything" produces a wiki page nobody reads.

**5 → Give them a genuinely good exit.** They're a future reference, a possible rehire, and a recruiter for you either way. The team is watching how you treat someone on their way out and drawing conclusions about how they'd be treated.

**Warning: don't redistribute their work this week.** Everyone's rattled and volunteering, and commitments made in that mood turn into resentment within a month. Say out loud that coverage gets decided next week, once the transfer list exists.

**A 504 means a proxy in front of your app gave up waiting for a response, so the problem is downstream of whatever returned it.** Something answered you, so the network path works. It's slow or stuck, not absent.

**1 → The 504 came from a proxy, and that names your first suspect.** Nginx, a load balancer, an API gateway, a CDN. That box was healthy enough to write you an error. Response headers usually tell you which one it was.

**2 → It means "no response within my timeout", not "the app is down".** Down gives you a 502 or a refused connection. A 504 usually means the request did reach your app and may still be running there, long after the client saw the error. Look in the app logs for a request with a start line and no finish line.

**3 → The timeout value is what makes this actionable, so know yours.** Nginx `proxy_read_timeout` defaults to 60s, AWS ALB is 60s, Cloudflare is 100s on free and pro plans. Requests failing at exactly that number are genuinely slow requests. Requests failing at wildly varying times are something else, usually a hung upstream connection or a saturated pool.

**4 → In a chain of proxies, you only see the outermost 504.** CDN in front of a load balancer in front of a gateway means the timeout that actually fired could be three hops in. Timeouts should get shorter as you move toward the app, and when they don't you get exactly this kind of confusing failure.

**Warning: raising the timeout is almost never the fix.** It converts a fast failure into a slow one and lets in-flight connections pile up until the proxy exhausts its worker pool, which takes down endpoints that were fine. Find why the request takes that long: usually a slow query, an outbound call with no timeout of its own, or a starved connection pool.

**Also found:** if the 504s cluster on one endpoint, it's that code path. If they're spread evenly across all endpoints, it's something shared, so look at the database, the connection pool, or CPU saturation.

**Dual-write to the new table, backfill history in throttled batches, then flip reads behind a flag.** That's the whole shape, and on 200GB it's days to weeks of elapsed time, not one night.

**1 → Create the new table and start dual-writing before you copy anything.** Every insert, update, and delete on the old table also lands on the new one, via triggers or in the application. Do this first, or you'll spend the backfill chasing rows that changed while you were copying them.

**2 → Backfill in batches by primary key range, with a pause between batches.** Roughly 10k rows per batch is a sane starting point. Make each batch an upsert (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`) so it's safe to re-run and safe when it collides with a live dual write. Record the last key processed in a table so a crash resumes instead of restarting from zero.

**3 → Verify before you trust it.** Row counts first, then a checksum on a sample, then the full comparison if you can afford the scan. Run it after the backfill completes and dual-write has been going for a while. Expect a handful of mismatches at the boundary between backfill and live writes, and investigate every single one rather than waving them off as noise.

**4 → Flip reads gradually behind a flag: 1%, then 10%, then all.** Keep writing to both tables the whole time. If something's wrong you flip back in seconds instead of restoring a backup at 2am.

**5 → Only stop dual writes after a soak of at least a week.** Then rename the old table rather than dropping it, so recovery is a rename back rather than a restore. Drop it a month later.

**Warning: watch WAL volume and replica lag the entire backfill.** Batch-rewriting 200GB generates enormous WAL, and it will fill disk on the primary, stall replicas, and break logical replication or CDC downstream. Throttle batch size and sleep to keep replica lag under a few seconds. This is the thing that actually causes the outage you were trying to avoid, more often than the migration itself.

**Warning 2: check whether you need any of this first.** In Postgres 11+, `ADD COLUMN` with a default is instant, and many `ALTER` operations no longer rewrite the table. Only some changes genuinely require a rewrite: type changes, adding `NOT NULL` to existing data, and reordering columns. Confirm yours does before building a pipeline.

**Also found:** `pg_repack` handles online physical rewrites (bloat, re-clustering) with none of the above. It won't help with a real shape change, but it's worth ruling in or out before you start.
